CHINA AIRWAYS FEDERAL INC. U. S. A.
CABLE ADDRESS: "PACAMAIR"
51 CANTON ROAD
SHANGHAI
Personal
Mr.
S.1P. Morgan,
Pacific American
Airways,
135 East Forty-second St.,
New York City, N.Y.
Dear Mr. Morgan,
29 August, 1935
I like Chinese chow and frequently work
out with the sticks but there are times when it is a bit trying.-
I am enclosing an invitation from Mr.
M.Y. Tang and a menu of the dinner.
You will note item four
on
the menu.
It is considered polite
among Chinese to use your own
sticks (which, of course, you constantly put in your mouth) to
remove choice
morseis Irom the center, common source of supply.
ecause I don't like to eat food which others have deposited witł
their chop sticks on my plate I am always extremely polite and
usually manage to beat them to the draw. That system worked very
well the other night until the fourth item on the menu came along.
Then, while I was
waiting on Mrs. Tang,
the Chinese lady on my
left
waited on me by depositing on my plate the foot of a chicken,
a great delicacy, which I had to devour or lose a lot of face,
in fact, be quite insulting.
So far as flavor, for which chicken
doncernea - would much rather work out on an
ınner tube, which, rüns about as much but under more sanitary con-
ditions than a Chinese chicken.
When I was in Kweiyang with Communists
attacking the city I worried a lot as to whether I should let
the airplane fly away without me so as to see Chiang Kai Shek or
go with the plane.
Finally, when the missionaries decided to
leave I made up my mind that if the missionaries wouldn't stick
it out for Jesus that there was no particular point in my sticking
it
ar neck out for Juan.
I'm glad that the Communists were eventu-
ally defeated but I'm still sorry that that chicken was.
Sincerely,
H.M. Bixby

properties.sfomuseum:description: Typewritten letter from Harold M. Bixby to S. [Stokely] W. Morgan, dated August 29, 1935, on China Airways Federal Inc., labeled “Personal”; includes description of dining customs at a dinner with M.Y. and Mrs. Tang, brief mention of decision to leave Kweiyang [Guiyang] ahead of Long March; mentions Chiang Kai-shek and Juan [Trippe].
